Chapter 4: Building the First Personal Computer and Facing Doubt.
Picture this—the garage is alive with the hum of soldering irons, the steady clack of keyboards, and the quiet excitement of something new taking shape. That’s where our friends poured their hearts into building a computer small enough to sit on a desk, simple enough to run basic programs, and—most importantly—something anyone with a little patience could put together.
Every night brought its own hurdles. Circuits that stubbornly refused to work, parts that just wouldn’t fit, and that nagging question in the back of their minds—what if this is all just a wild goose chase?
Most people around them just didn't get it. Back then, computers were these mysterious, mega-expensive machines that belonged in big companies or universities. Their families and friends meant well, but you could hear the doubt in their voices. Why spend all this time and money on something so unlikely? Was chasing this dream just setting themselves up for disappointment?
But the friends kept at it. What pushed them forward? This simple, powerful idea: technology should be for everyone. They got creative—finding cheaper parts, designing their own circuit boards, and writing code that squeezed the most out of what little they had. Every setback taught them something new, and every small win fueled their determination to keep going.
One of the toughest things? Convincing the world their project actually mattered. They started bringing their prototype to local computer clubs, hoping to connect with folks who might be just as excited. At first, the response was... well, let’s just say it was underwhelming. A few hobbyists were curious, but most people just didn’t see the point. Why would anyone want a computer at home? What could you possibly do with it?
That’s when they realized—building the machine was only half the battle. The real challenge was showing people what this technology could do, making it feel fun and approachable. So, they started giving live demos, letting people try the computer for themselves. And slowly, something started to change. Curiosity turned into excitement. People began to imagine new possibilities—playing games, writing stories, even creating art. The idea of a personal computer was finally starting to catch on.
With growing interest came new pressures. They needed money to build more machines, and had to figure out how to turn their passion project into a real business. That meant tough choices—how much to charge, how to handle orders, and who would take on which jobs. Through it all, they leaned on each other, trusting the bond they’d built over years of working together.
Most folks don’t see what it’s like to be first. There were plenty of moments when doubt crept in—times when quitting seemed a whole lot easier. But the friends pushed forward, holding onto the belief that they were making something that truly mattered. The whole process was messy, full of mistakes and false starts, but every challenge brought them one step closer to their dream.
